newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, UPS prepare to renew contract talks.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, UPS prepare to renew contract talks.

text.p: The Teamsters and United Parcel Service head to the bargaining table for the first time in four days on Thursday in hopes of ending a national walkout that has crippled the giant parcel delivery company.

Management and union officials were set to meet with a federal mediator in Washington to address unresolved issues ranging from pay and benefits to the company's use of non-union subcontractors and part-time workers.

News of a renewal in negotiations held out hope to businesses, manufacturers and other UPS customers, who have had to reckon with higher shipping costs and logistical nightmares to get their parcels delivered.

But Teamster President Ron Carey was sceptical about the likelihood that negotiations would produce a settlement in the decade's biggest U.S. labour strike. "We have seen no sign that the company has changed its attitude, so we are not particularly optimistic about these new talks," Carey said late on Wednesday.

Chief UPS negotiator Dave Murray flew to Washington from Atlanta on Wednesday evening to represent the company at the talks. But the company said it was not backing away from management's latest proposal, which Teamster leaders have already rejected.
"UPS remains committed to its final contract offer and is encouraging the union leaders to let UPS Teamsters vote on the proposal," a company statement said.

The strike by 185,000 Teamsters began at a minute past midnight EDT on Monday (0401 GMT), after a last-ditch effort to avoid a work stoppage collapsed. The two sides sat through 17 hours of talks with a mediator but wound up deadlocked.

Since then UPS has been handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments by re-assigning 50,000 non-union employees to field jobs. The company also said that more than 5,000 Teamster members had decided not to join the strike and were crossing union picket lines.
The two sides agreed to meet after days of pressure from the Clinton administration, though the White House has resisted calls to use its executive authority to end the strike.
Business leaders warned of irreparable harm and massive layoffs for small- and mid-size firms if the strikers were not ordered back to work.

But Clinton told a White House news conference he could only intervene in the job action by invoking the rarely used Taft-Hartley Law, which authorises the nation's chief executive to halt strikes that threaten health and safety.
"There has to be a severe damage to the country. The test is ... very high before the president can intervene," he said.
Labour Secretary Alexis Herman spoke with UPS Chairman James Kelly and Carey on Wednesday and said she was "encouraged" the two sides had agreed to meet.
"The president and I feel strongly that both the company and the workers, as well as the American people, have much to gain in a quick resolution to this dispute," she said.

The Teamsters blamed the strike on a company refusal to end sub-contracting and create thousands of new full-time jobs each year from part-time jobs, which account for 60 percent of the Atlanta-based company's 301,000 domestic workers.

UPS called those issues "a smoke screen," saying the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a multi-employer pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms.
